title: Pipeline for 2-photon all-optical physiology in mouse: From viral titration and optical window implantation to binarization of calcium transients
protocol: Read and adhere to the safety instructions for handling AAVs or other viruses from your institution.
Dilute the calcium indicator virus in sterile PBS according to desired titer: undiluted, 1:20, 1:40.
Dilute the opsin virus in sterile PBS according to desired titer: undiluted, 2:1, 1:1.
Store diluted viruses at 4°C protected from light for up to 2 weeks.
Mix calcium indicator stock solution with opsin stock solution to create virus-pair solutions.
Pipette 1:20 titer of GCaMP6f and 2:1 titer of C1V1T/T in one tube.
Pipette 1:40 titer of GCaMP6f and 2:1 titer of C1V1T/T in another tube.
Pipette 1:20 titer of GCaMP6f and 4:1 titer of C1V1T/T in a third tube.
Store all tubes at 4°C avoiding light exposure.
Weigh the animal.
Anesthetize the animal by placing it in an anesthesia induction chamber with 4% Isoflurane/oxygen.
Wait until the breathing rate drops to approximately 60 BPM.
Administer local analgesia by injecting buprenorphine subcutaneously at a concentration of 0.05–0.1 mg/kg.
Transfer the deeply anesthetized animal to the stereotaxic frame.
Position the upper front teeth into the dedicated opening of the tooth bar.
Cover the nose with the anesthesia mask if volatile anesthetics are used and ensure it fits tightly.
Set the isoflurane level typically to 2%.
Test the animal’s reflexes by pinching the skin between the toes with a forceps.
Increase the anesthesia slowly if reflexes are observed.
Insert the temperature sensor into the rectum of the animal.
Set the desired temperature value between 37°C and 38°C.
Observe respiration carefully.
Ensure respiration rate exceeds 30 breaths per minute during surgery.
Apply dexpanthenol eye cream to prevent drying of the eyes.
Apply 2% xylocaine solution on the surgical area several minutes before surgery.
Shave the head with an electric hair trimmer, ensuring a larger shaved area than the actual opening.
Clean the shaved area thoroughly after shaving.
Fix the animal's head firmly using ear bars and check alignment.
Cut the scalp at the midline sagittal suture with a scalpel blade.
Pull aside the scalp to expose the skull.
Peel or cut off the periosteum from the skull.
Clean and expose the skull using triangle sponges.
Attach an 18G needle to the stereotaxic frame.
Match the tip of the needle to bregma.
Set the coordinates of the micromanipulator to zero.
Move the tip of the needle to the injection point according to the desired coordinates for visual cortex (anterior posterior 3.0 mm and medial lateral 2.8 mm).
Mark the position on the skull using ink administered on the tip of the needle.
Thin the skull at the respective location using a dental drill with a 0.5 mm diameter bit.
Perform the craniotomy to access the brain for virus injection.
Drill very slowly and carefully when approaching the skull to avoid puncturing the brain.
Pour saline or PBS on the drilling site every 2–3 minutes to prevent heating damage.
Gently lift up the thinned skull fragment using a 20G needle or fine tip forceps.
Cover the opening area with saline or PBS, or surgical sponge soaked in these solutions, throughout surgery to prevent dehydration and tissue damage.
Exchange the 18G needle for a pulled micropipette in the stereotaxic frame.
Connect the syringe to the micropipette using tubing for manual loading and injection of virus solution.
Mount the micropipette to the arm of the stereotaxic frame in the correct angle and coordinate.
Place a piece of parafilm onto the animal’s head.
Drop 1 μL of the virus solution on the parafilm.
Lower the micropipette tip into the drop of the solution.
Apply negative pressure via the syringe to front-load the micropipette with the virus solution.
Withdraw the micropipette by operating the micromanipulator after loading.
Remove the parafilm from the animal’s head.
Position the micropipette containing the solution at the injection site, 250 μm deep in the brain.
Administer the virus at a depth of 250 μm with an angle of 35°.
Move the micropipette to 200 μm and administer the virus again with an angle of 35°.
Move the micropipette further down to 150 μm and inject the virus once more with an angle of 35°.
Place a disinfected piece of parafilm on the top of the surgical sponge covering the craniotomy.
Lower the tip of the micropipette at an angle of 35° for the injection.
Apply a drop of virus solution (1.0 μL) onto the parafilmed surface.
Maintain the virus solution at 4°C until application.
Load the virus into the micropipette using the micromanipulator to reach 0.6 μL volume.
Gently retract the micropipette after loading.
Remove the parafilm and position the micropipette back onto the surface of the brain for injection.
Reset the z-axis of the micromanipulator to zero.
Advance the micropipette slowly into the brain (ca. 150–250 μm in z-coordinate).
Use a total volume of 0.6 μL for injection.
Administer 200 nL virus volume at each injection point.
Inject the virus solution at three depths along the injection site: 250 μm, 200 μm, and 150 μm with an angle of 35°.
Apply pressure onto the syringe to inject the virus solution into the brain.
Control the speed of injection by observing ink markers on the micropipette and regulating pressure in parallel.
Maintain the injection rate at ≤ 0.20 μL/min.
Keep the micropipette in place for another 5–10 min after finishing the injection.
Withdraw the micropipette slowly.
Clean the injection point with saline/PBS.
Put the scalp back to its original place and suture it or front-load a micropipette with surgical glue for sealing the incision.
Carefully move the scalp back to its original position using a triangle sponge.
Glue the skin using surgical glue.
Move the glued skin from one side to another to ensure it is not adhered to the skull.
Administer surgical glue on the incision carefully, ensuring no glue gets under the skin.
Cut the tip of a pulled micropipette with a small spring scissor to create an opening of approximately 0.5 mm.
Dip the pipette into a surgical glue drop; capillary forces will suck the glue into the micropipette.
Transcardially perfuse the animal with PBS to remove blood residues.
Switch the perfusion solution to 4% PFA for tissue fixation.
Remove the brain without damaging it and post-fix it in 4% PFA for 24 hours.
After 24 hours, transfer the brain to a falcon tube containing 15% sucrose.
Incubate the tissue in 15% sucrose for 24 hours.
Transfer the tissue to a new falcon tube containing 30% sucrose.
Incubate the tissue in 30% sucrose for another 24 hours.
Slice the brain region of interest (70 μm thickness) using a Vibratome.
Cut the brain into coronal slices.
Transfer the slices directly onto object slides.
Mark the slices with a nucleic acid stain shortly before mounting, e.g., DAPI.
Mount the slice with Vectashield Mounting Medium.
Cover the mounted slice with a cover slip.
Make an incision: cut the scalp with a scalpel blade at the midline sagittal suture.
Use a small spring scissor to partially remove the scalp from the skull.
Peel off the periosteum and clean the skull thoroughly with sponge and PBS.
Ink-mark the tip of a needle to locate the bregma for defining the zero-position of the micromanipulator.
Ensure the exposed skull surface is smaller than the shaved region.
Clean the exposed skull with triangle sponges drenched in PBS.
Use a scalpel blade to carefully scratch any remaining tissue/fascia from the skull.
Peel or cut off the periosteum.
Scratch and clean the skull surface thoroughly for adhesion of adhesive.
Attach an 18G needle to the stereotaxic frame and match its tip to bregma.
Set the micromanipulator coordinates to zero.
Place a piece of surgical sponge soaked in PBS/Saline on top of the injection site and keep it there for a few minutes.
Remove the sponge from the injection site.
Use a biopsy puncher to make a very shallow cut around the central point of the injection site as a landmark.
Front-load a micropipette with surgical glue.
Seal the edges of the skin surrounding the exposed skull.
Drill the skull carefully according to the biopsy puncher mark to thin out the bone but without punctuating the brain.
Clean the surface from the bone scrapings with compressed air.
Moisturize the skull with wet surgical sponges from time to time.
Thin the skull out with a dental drill at the ledger line previously marked.
Remove the thinned skull remains with forceps to expose the brain.
Apply PBS or saline on the exposed brain to keep it hydrated.
Load the virus into the micropipette.
Administer the virus into the exposed brain according to the desired coordinate.
Place cover glass onto the opened skull.
Seal the edges of the cover glass with surgical glue delivered via a micropipette.
Maintain pressure upright until the glue is dry.
Front-load a micropipette for virus injection according to steps 5a–e from “protocol part 1”.
Pull aside the surgical sponge to perform the virus injection as per steps 5f–j from “protocol part 1”.
Clean the injection point with saline/PBS carefully.
Cover exposed brain tissue with PBS/Saline or a wet surgical sponge throughout the procedure.
Front-load a micropipette with surgical glue for gluing the coverslip in step 7r.
Take a coverslip with a diameter of 3 or 4 mm and a thickness of 0.1 mm using small forceps.
Clean the coverslip with a triangle sponge and ethanol 70%.
Float the cleaned coverslip in PBS/Saline solution.
Remove the surgical sponge from the exposed tissue and moisten the area with PBS/Saline drop.
Place the coverslip over the opening area of the skull.
Gently press the coverslip on the skull with an angled forceps to adhere it completely to the bone.
Use triangle sponges to carefully dry the skull around the coverslip without soaking up the PBS/Saline under the coverslip while applying gentle pressure with an angled forceps.
Check for air bubbles between the tissue and the coverslip, ensuring no air is present for successful imaging.
Apply small amounts of surgical glue point after point all around the coverslip using a micropipette while maintaining gentle pressure with an angled forceps.
Maintain pressure by the angled forceps for approximately 2 minutes until the glue is dry.
If the remaining exposed skull is wet, dry it properly using Q-tips and triangle sponges.
Gently make small incisions on the skull surface in a grid pattern with a scalpel blade for improved adhesion.
Use a scalpel blade to cut small incisions forming a grid pattern on the exposed skull.
Apply UV-glue in layers onto the skull.
Harden each layer of UV-glue with UV-light after placement.
Implant the holder by gluing it onto the last layers of UV-glue applied.
Prepare the adhesive (dental cement or UV-glue) for application.
Use a 20G needle to apply the adhesive only on the exposed skull, avoiding the skin.
Mix cement appropriately to ensure neither fluidity nor density extremes.
Apply UV-glue in small layers.
Expose each layer of UV-glue to UV-light after application.
Avoid applying a large amount of UV-glue at once to prevent uneven hardening.
Cover only the borders of the coverslip with adhesive.
Do not apply adhesive on top of the coverslip.
Attach the metal head holder to the animal’s skull using adhesive.
Apply some glue to the base of the head holder and place it onto previously applied UV glue layer.
Ensure that the adhesive is completely dry before moving the animal from the stereotaxic frame.
Prepare a dedicated hardware setup for all-optical experiments.
Photostimulate opsin-expressing cells using the setup.
Ensure that excitation wavelengths are sufficiently separated to avoid cross-talk between imaging channels.
Transfer the animal to the microscope.
Mount the headholder to a restraining device under the microscopes’ objective.
Habituate animals prior to imaging sessions if experiments are conducted in awake conditions.
Handle the animal for 15–20 minutes on each of the first two days.
Restrain the animal’s head on day three and four.
Restraining under the microscope without imaging occurs on day five.
Use a femtosecond pulsed laser and resonant scanner for fast full-field scanning up to 35 Hz.
Employ a Titan-Sapphire (Ti:Sa) laser at 920 nm for calcium indicator expressing cells imaging.
Define regions of interest (ROI) for photostimulation.
Adapt pixel dwell times and line width settings.
Adjust the recorded field of view for functional calcium imaging.
Set sensitivity of PMTs.
Select wavelength of the laser for calcium indicator excitation.
Control shutters for laser operation.
Modify properties of lasers for photostimulation.
Set wavelength of the laser for opsin excitation.
Use an independent laser for opsin excitation.
Pump the optical parametric oscillator (OPO) at 1100 nm with a Ti:Sa laser at 800 nm.
Employ a second galvo-resonant mirror system or spatial light modulator to achieve longer pixel dwell times.
Equip the first PMT with a spectral bandpass filter matching the emission properties of the calcium indicator.
Operate a second PMT with a bandpass filter that matches the fluorescence reporter properties of the opsin.
Carry out ROI-based raster-scan stimulation on previously identified co-expressing cells.
Measure the point spread function (PSF) as part of regular quality control for the microscope.
Export imaging data as a series of single tiffs or tiff stack.
Compensate for motion artefacts in x–y direction using the moco plugin of ImageJ.
Select a reference image from the time-lapse series that contains a high amount of visible neurons.
Alternatively, calculate an average intensity projection of the entire time-series using the “z-project” function in ImageJ and choose “average” projection.
Use other projection types if necessary, such as maximum or median intensity projection, depending on the quality of your recording.
Load motion-corrected single tiffs or tiff stacks into Matlab.
Calculate an average intensity projection based on the stated number of frames.
Mark all identifiable neurons in the projection using polygon shapes, defining them as ROIs.
Adjust brightness properties of the projection if necessary to simplify neuron identification.
State the dimensions of the field of view in μm.
Report the sample rate of the image acquisition.
Label each soma by drawing a polygon around its border for all visible neurons in the field of view.
Calculate the averaged intensity of the enclosed pixels over time for each region of interest (ROI).
Display the calculated intensity as an intensity trace.
Define a baseline free of activity for each intensity trace, indicated by green dashed boxes.
Represent the change in fluorescence for each neuron as a series of values in an array.
Average all intensity values of all pixels within each ROI for every image in the series or tiff stack.
Define a 10 s long period of quiescence characterized by the absence of functional calcium transient or signal fluctuations as baseline F0 separately for each neuron.
Calculate the relative change of fluorescence for each time point using ΔF = (F - F0) / F0.
Calculate the relative change in fluorescence to determine calcium transients.
Load data into IGOR Pro for analysis.
Smooth each intensity trace using a Gaussian filter.
Inspect traces for ongoing neuronal activity during measurement.
Manually exclude unwanted or falsely identified structures from further analysis.
For peak identification of calcium transients, ensure that the first derivative of the amplitude crosses zero.
Ensure that the second derivative is negative at the point where the first derivative crosses zero.
Identify the onset of the calcium transient as the first data point dropping below 0.5 SD of the baseline.
Fit an exponential curve to the trace after the peak to mimic the τ off of the calcium indicator.
Determine the offset by identifying the data point when the fitted curve reaches 0.5 SD of the baseline.
Manually correct peak locations if necessary and lacking a priori knowledge of calcium indicator dynamics.
Binarize intensity traces so that peaks are represented as 1 and periods of quiescence as 0.
